::: {.eyebrow}
reference · terms
:::

The guides and theory pages use these words in the specific senses below. Where
a word has an everyday or wider-literature meaning that differs, the entry says
so. Each term has an anchor, so pages can link straight to it, for example
`glossary.qmd#node`.

::: {.callout-note}
## Model and strategy

`plant` is renaming its rule-set classes from *strategy* to *model*
([plant#641](https://github.com/traitecoevo/plant/issues/641)). This glossary
already uses the new vocabulary: a **model** is FF16, TF24, TF24f, or K93, and a
**strategy** is one species' trait values. Until the rename lands, the code
still calls the rule set a strategy, as in `FF16_Strategy`,
`strategy_default()`, and `Individual$strategy`.
:::

## Models, parameters, and traits

[Model]{#model}
:   The equations that map a plant's traits, size, and environment to growth,
    fecundity, mortality, and its effect on competition. `plant` ships FF16,
    TF24, TF24f, and K93.

[Parameters]{#parameters}
:   The constants a model needs that are shared across every species in a run,
    such as the light-extinction coefficient or the disturbance regime.

[Strategy]{#strategy}
:   One species' set of trait values: a point in trait space. Evolution and
    community assembly act on strategies. "The TF24 model, run with three
    strategies" is the intended usage.

[Trait]{#trait}
:   A measurable plant property that differs between strategies, such as leaf
    mass per area (LMA) or wood density. Traits enter a model only through its
    parameters, usually via a hyperparameterisation.

[Hyperparameterisation]{#hyperparameterisation}
:   An R function that turns a small set of traits into a consistent set of
    model parameters, encoding links between traits (for example, LMA also sets
    leaf turnover). FF16's is `FF16_hyperpar()`.

[Individual]{#individual}
:   One plant, following a model with one strategy. Its state includes a size
    coordinate — height for FF16 and TF24, stem diameter for K93 — and, for some
    models, further physiological state.

## Size structure and nodes

[Size distribution]{#size-distribution}
:   The density of plants across the size coordinate, for one strategy, in one
    patch at one patch age. For K93 the size coordinate is stem diameter, but
    the solver still stores it in a column named `height`.

[Characteristic]{#characteristic}
:   The path through size and patch age traced by plants born at one instant.
    Following characteristics turns the size-structured PDE into ODEs along each
    path; see [the characteristic
    method](theory/implementation/characteristic-method.qmd).

[Node]{#node}
:   A numerical point that samples the size distribution of one strategy at one
    recruitment time. A node follows one characteristic, carrying a size and a
    density per unit recruitment time. Nodes are the objects the solver
    introduces, steps forward, and plots as lines.

[Cohort]{#cohort}
:   The plants of one strategy recruited between two adjacent nodes. A cohort's
    abundance is the node density integrated over that interval of recruitment
    times, which the solver approximates with the trapezium rule; this is why
    node spacing matters. Not "each node represents a cohort": in an escalator
    boxcar train a cohort is a point mass, but `plant` is a density method; see
    [Size or age](posts/2026-08-04-size-or-age-coordinates/index.qmd).

[Node-introduction schedule]{#node-introduction-schedule}
:   The recruitment times at which the solver introduces new nodes.
    `run_scm(..., refine_schedule = TRUE)` refines it adaptively, adding nodes
    where removing one would make a population integral too inaccurate
    (threshold `schedule_eps`); see [node
    spacing](theory/implementation/node-spacing.qmd). Refining the schedule
    improves numerical accuracy; it does not change birth rates.

[SCM]{#scm}
:   The deterministic solver that integrates a patch's size distributions along
    characteristics, run with `run_scm()`. `plant` also has a stochastic,
    finite-population solver that tracks individuals.

## Patches and the landscape

[Patch]{#patch}
:   A local community of competing plants, followed from one disturbance
    onward. A patch starts empty unless it is
    [initialised](guides/initialising-a-patch.qmd) with a population.

[Patch age]{#patch-age}
:   Time since the patch was last disturbed. The solver runs one patch
    trajectory, so patch age is also its time coordinate.

[Disturbance]{#disturbance}
:   A stand-replacing event that removes all plants and resets patch age to
    zero. The default regime is Weibull with a fixed shape, parameterised by
    `max_patch_lifetime`.

[Patch-age distribution]{#patch-age-distribution}
:   How common patches of each age are in the landscape under the disturbance
    regime. Landscape averages are patch outputs weighted by this distribution.

[Metacommunity]{#metacommunity}
:   The landscape of patches of different ages, linked by a shared pool of
    dispersing seeds. It is implicit: one patch trajectory supplies the state at
    every patch age, and no separate object is created per patch.

[Competitive environment]{#competitive-environment}
:   The shared quantity through which plants affect each other: the canopy-light
    profile for FF16 and TF24 (plus soil water where it is simulated), or the
    basal area of larger neighbours for K93.

[Canopy openness]{#canopy-openness}
:   The fraction of open-sky light reaching a given height in the canopy, set by
    the leaf area above that height through Beer's law.

## Demography and equilibrium

[Birth rate]{#birth-rate}
:   The rate at which seeds of a strategy arrive in a patch. Older code and
    papers call this *seed rain*.

[Offspring production]{#offspring-production}
:   The dispersing seeds a strategy produces, integrated across its plants and
    across patch ages.

[Net reproduction ratio]{#net-reproduction-ratio}
:   Offspring production per incoming seed. `run_scm()` reports it for each
    strategy; a value of one means the strategy exactly replaces itself.

[Demographic equilibrium]{#demographic-equilibrium}
:   A state in which each resident's seed output matches its seed input, so its
    net reproduction ratio is one. Finding it is a fixed-point search over birth
    rates, separate from running one patch.

## Adaptive dynamics

[Adaptive dynamics]{#adaptive-dynamics}
:   The framework for asking how traits evolve when evolution proceeds by rare
    mutants with small trait differences invading a resident community at
    demographic equilibrium. See [adaptive
    dynamics](theory/adaptive-dynamics.qmd).

[Resident]{#resident}
:   A strategy that is already established, at demographic equilibrium, and sets
    the competitive environment.

[Mutant]{#mutant}
:   A rare new strategy, assumed too rare to change the residents' competitive
    environment.

[Invasion fitness]{#invasion-fitness}
:   The long-term per-capita growth rate of a rare mutant in the residents'
    environment. At demographic equilibrium, `plant` uses the mutant's basic
    reproduction ratio, which gives the same ordering of strategies.

[Basic reproduction ratio]{#basic-reproduction-ratio}
:   $R(x', x)$: the expected number of dispersing seeds ultimately produced by
    one dispersing seed of mutant $x'$ among residents $x$. The mutant can
    invade if $R > 1$.

[Fitness landscape]{#fitness-landscape}
:   Invasion fitness as a function of mutant trait values, for a fixed set of
    residents.

[Pairwise invasibility plot (PIP)]{#pip}
:   A map over resident trait (one axis) and mutant trait (the other) showing
    where the mutant can invade. Singular strategies and their stability can be
    read off its shape.

[Selection gradient]{#selection-gradient}
:   The slope of invasion fitness with respect to the mutant's trait, evaluated
    at the resident's trait value. A positive gradient favours mutants with a
    slightly larger trait value, a negative one slightly smaller.

[Singular strategy]{#singular-strategy}
:   A strategy at which the selection gradient is zero, so gradual evolution
    pushes the trait neither up nor down.

[Evolutionarily stable strategy (ESS)]{#ess}
:   A resident strategy that no nearby mutant can invade: it sits at a maximum
    of its own fitness landscape.

[Convergence stable]{#convergence-stable}
:   A singular strategy that gradual evolution approaches from nearby trait
    values. Convergence stability and evolutionary stability are independent:
    a strategy can have either without the other.

[Evolutionary attractor]{#evolutionary-attractor}
:   A convergence-stable singular strategy: where gradual evolution heads. If it
    is also an ESS, evolution stops there. `regnans` finds attractors with
    `community_solve_singularity()`.

[Evolutionary branching point]{#branching-point}
:   A convergence-stable singular strategy that is not an ESS. Evolution
    approaches it, then nearby mutants on both sides can invade, and the
    population can split into two strategies.

[Community assembly]{#community-assembly}
:   Building a multi-strategy community step by step: add the mutant with the
    highest invasion fitness, return the community to demographic equilibrium,
    remove any resident that goes extinct, and repeat. See [community
    assembly](theory/adaptive-dynamics/assembly.qmd).

## Numerical methods

[ODE]{#ode}
:   Ordinary differential equation: a rate of change with respect to one
    variable, here time. Each node's size, survival, and seed production follow
    ODEs.

[PDE]{#pde}
:   Partial differential equation: rates of change with respect to more than
    one variable. The [size-structured PDE](theory/size-structured-pde.qmd)
    describes how the size distribution changes in both size and patch age;
    following characteristics turns it into ODEs.

[Step]{#step}
:   One advance of every ODE state from time $t$ to $t + h$, where $h$ is the
    step size.

[Stepper]{#stepper}
:   The numerical method that takes one step and estimates that step's error,
    such as RK45.

[Solver]{#solver}
:   The code that drives a stepper across an interval, choosing each step size
    to keep the error within tolerance and stopping at the times requested.
    `plant` uses `odelia::ode::Solver`; the SCM wraps it, introducing nodes and
    updating the competitive environment between steps.

[RK45]{#rk45}
:   The Cash–Karp Runge–Kutta 4(5) stepper, `plant`'s default. It is explicit
    and adaptive: each step's fourth- and fifth-order estimates are compared to
    measure error and set the next step size. Setting `fixed_time_step` switches
    to fixed steps; see [ODE stepping](theory/implementation/ode-stepping.qmd).

[Error tolerance]{#error-tolerance}
:   The local error the solver accepts per step, set by `ode_tol_rel` and
    `ode_tol_abs`. Tighter tolerances mean smaller steps and more work.

[Explicit and implicit methods]{#explicit-implicit}
:   An explicit method computes the next state directly from the current state
    and its rates; an implicit method solves an equation involving the next
    state too. Implicit methods cost more per step but stay stable on stiff
    systems.

[Stiff system]{#stiff-system}
:   An ODE system whose processes run on very different time scales, so an
    explicit stepper needs impractically small steps to stay stable. Adding
    soil water (the Richards equation) to `plant` made its system stiff, as did
    continuous seed feedback in a reimplementation of FF16.

[Trapezium rule]{#trapezium-rule}
:   Quadrature that joins neighbouring points with straight lines. `plant` uses
    it to integrate over nodes, such as leaf area above a height or a cohort's
    abundance, so its accuracy depends on node spacing.

[Spline]{#spline}
:   A smooth piecewise curve fitted through sampled points. `plant` computes
    canopy openness at an adaptively chosen set of heights and evaluates a
    spline elsewhere, rather than recomputing it for every node.

[Finite difference]{#finite-difference}
:   A derivative estimated from function values at nearby points. `plant` uses
    it for the growth-rate derivative $\partial g / \partial H$ in the
    characteristic equation, optionally improved by Richardson extrapolation.

## Packages

[plant]{#plant}
:   The R package these pages document: size-, trait-, and patch-structured
    forest models (FF16, TF24, TF24f, K93), solved with the method of
    characteristics or as a stochastic, finite population.
    [Source](https://github.com/traitecoevo/plant).

[odelia]{#odelia}
:   A C++ header library, with an R interface, for solving ODEs. It provides
    `plant`'s adaptive solver and steppers, an implicit Rosenbrock stepper for
    stiff systems, interpolators, and support for automatic differentiation.
    [Source](https://github.com/traitecoevo/odelia).

[regnans]{#regnans}
:   An R package for community assembly and adaptive dynamics with `plant`: it
    iterates demography to equilibrium, computes selection gradients and
    invasion fitness, and solves for evolutionary attractors. It also includes
    four small models with explicit solutions ([models in
    regnans](theory/adaptive-dynamics/index.qmd)).
    [Source](https://github.com/traitecoevo/regnans).

[phylloptim]{#phylloptim}
:   An R package and C++ headers for leaf gas exchange with explicit plant
    hydraulics, extracted from the TF24 model so that it can be tested and
    reused on its own. In current `plant` (the `develop` branch), TF24 calls it
    for its leaf-level calculations.
    [Source](https://github.com/traitecoevo/phylloptim).
